prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, bringing atomic frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: After reading the full set of opening ballots I move my preferred configuration from circuit QED (my opening first place) to optical lattice clocks. The case is that B006 is the one candidate that is both broadly supported (ranked by seven of eight members, two first places, four top-three placements) and robust on every criterion I care about. The magic-wavelength lattice idea is a single clear physical insight, the 10^-18 performance has been reproduced and surpassed in several independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE), and every systematic effect can be traced to a physical detail, which is the kind of control I value. The discovery has already opened measurable new regimes: gravitational redshift across millimetre-scale samples, searches for variation of constants and dark matter, and a credible path to redefining the second. The two-name credit (Katori for the concept and first strontium lattice clocks, Ye for taking accuracy, stability and many-body clock physics to the record level) is clean and fits the prize limit without leaving a conspicuous gap.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is partly a precision-measurement and metrology achievement that follows the 2005 frequency-comb prize (Hall and Hansch) and the 2012 recognition of ion manipulation and ion clocks (Wineland), so a sceptic can call it an extraordinary refinement of a recognised line rather than a new discovery of nature. There is also a genuine allocation issue: Ludlow, Lemonde, Hinkley and the Yb and ion-clock communities all contributed to the 10^-18 milestone, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened. I also have to concede that my own field and my own first-place candidate, circuit QED, is the one I am least able to judge impartially.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked optical lattice clocks first as a precision-measurement achievement with a clean physical idea, quantitative control, a stable interpretation and timely relevance to the SI redefinition, and ranked circuit QED only sixth, citing the omission of Wallraff and the recent 2025 circuits prize.
responses.response: I agree with her on B006 and, on reflection, with both of her points about B015. Wallraff's first strong-coupling experiment is arguably decisive, and a prize naming Schoelkopf, Girvin and Blais would leave a visible hole that I cannot repair within the credited names. The 2025 prize also makes a second superconducting-circuit award feel too soon. Where I qualify her view is on weighting: the Katori idea versus the Ye-group performance record is not trivially settled, and I would keep the citation tied to the lattice-clock concept and its realisation rather than to the precision record alone.

responses.point: Pearce ranked IceCube first and the aberration-corrected electron microscope second, and put clocks third, noting that the Hall-Hansch comb prize of 2005 and Wineland's 2012 recognition make some members regard clocks as incremental.
responses.response: I take the overlap objection seriously but disagree that it makes clocks incremental. The comb and ion-trap prizes honoured tools and a different clock architecture, whereas the neutral-atom lattice clock, with many thousands of atoms interrogated simultaneously at a magic wavelength, brought a new regime of statistical power and many-body effects that none of those earlier works delivered. On B043 I defer to Pearce and Danielsson on astroparticle physics, but I note that the source identification is still partial, as several of us wrote, so it seems less settled than clocks on maturity.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked topological insulators first as a genuinely new state of matter in which theory predicted and experiment confirmed, and flagged that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe prediction is not among the credited names.
responses.response: I find B004 scientifically compelling and it is my main alternative, and I agree with her on the conceptual originality of the Z2 classification. My difficulty is the attribution that she and Mehlig also flag: the Kane-Mele, BHZ, Fu-Kane-Mele and Moore-Balents contributions interlock, and the 2016 topological-phases prize overlaps the conceptual core, so I am less certain than she is that the three credited names are complete. I would support it if condensed-matter colleagues convince me that the credit boundary can be drawn cleanly, because I defer to them on that.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked magic-angle graphene first because a clean continuum model predicted flat bands that experiments then confirmed, and also ranked cold-atom Hubbard simulation third, preferring model systems that can be controlled and analysed.
responses.response: I share his taste for controlled model systems, which is why B023 is my second choice, but I do not think it is ready as a single prize with three names. His own ballot picks Bloch, Cirac and Zoller whereas mine and Lindroth's pick Bloch, Greiner and Zoller, which shows how unsettled the allocation is, so the attribution problem is more serious here than for clocks. On B009 I agree that the theory-experiment link is striking, but the superconducting pairing mechanism is still debated, and I rate that as a maturity concern relative to the clocks.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will see optical lattice clocks as a new discovery or as an extraordinary refinement following the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes.
Whether Ludlow, Lemonde, Hinkley or ion-clock leaders should be weighed against Katori and Ye, and how the citation should be worded to cover this fairly.
Whether the Katori priority for the magic-wavelength concept and the Ye-group records are weighted equally; I have not verified individual priority claims independently.
Whether condensed-matter colleagues can resolve the Kane-Mele versus BHZ attribution for B004 well enough for it to overtake clocks, since I defer to them.
statement.conflict_note: Possible recusal issue on circuit QED (B015): I am a circuit-QED theorist who co-authors with experimentalists, and as director of WACQT I work closely with the Yale and ETH-linked community around Schoelkopf, Girvin, Blais and Wallraff, which is why I no longer prefer B015. I also have institutional ties to Chalmers colleagues in superconducting circuits. No specific personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye, or the other shortlisted candidates is apparent from my profile.
